1.title: Branching Strategies for Teams
1.text: Welcome to Module ten: Branching Strategies for Teams. It covers the exam area Part four: Git Hub collaboration. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Compare trunk-based development, Git Hub flow and Git Flow. Choose a strategy for a team. Run release branches and hotfixes. Name branches well. Explain the cost of long-lived branches. Tag releases with semantic versions. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Course
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the course. Part: Part four: Git Hub collaboration. Verified with: Git two point five zero.one for the local parts; the Git Hub documentation (read twenty twenty-six-eleven to sixteen) for the Git Hub parts.

1.title: What Was Executed and What Is Reference Only
1.text: What Was Executed and What Is Reference Only. Every Git command in this module was run for real in practice repositories. The Git Hub features come from the official Git Hub documentation and were not run.

1.title: Three strategies and the team each one fits
1.text: Three strategies and the team each one fits. A branching strategy is the team's agreement on which branches exist, how long they live and how work reaches users. The figure compares three common ones.

1.title: Three strategies and the team each one fits, continued
1.text: Three strategies and the team each one fits. The figure shows this: Three branching strategies side by side: trunk-based development with tiny branches, Git Hub flow with one branch per change, and Git Flow with main, develop, feature, release and hotfix branches.

1.title: Three strategies and the team each one fits, continued
1.text: Three strategies and the team each one fits. Trunk-based. Branches: main plus branches that live hours or a day or two. How work reaches users: Small changes merge to main at once; feature flags hide unfinished work. Git Hub flow. Branches: main plus one short branch per change. How work reaches users: Pull request, review, merge, deploy from main. Git Flow. Branches: main, develop, feature, release, hotfix. How work reaches users: Features go to develop, a release branch stabilizes, main holds releases.

1.title: Three strategies and the team each one fits, continued
1.text: Three strategies and the team each one fits. In trunk-based development the rule is small changes, merged often. A feature flag is a setting that the code checks, so unfinished code can sit in main while switched off. In the demo, a new checkout ships behind new checkout off, then a one-line change turns it on. Git Hub flow is the six steps of module nine, and main is always ready to deploy. Git Flow gives every branch a job.

1.title: Three strategies and the team each one fits, continued
1.text: Three strategies and the team each one fits. main. Job: Released code; every release gets a tag. Starts from: The first commit. Merges into: Nothing. develop. Job: Integration of the next release. Starts from: main. Merges into: main, through a release. feature slash. Job: One feature. Starts from: develop. Merges into: develop. release slash. Job: Stabilize a release: version bump, last fixes. Starts from: develop. Merges into: main and develop. hotfix slash. Job: Urgent fix to released code. Starts from: main. Merges into: main and develop. Try it. After one full cycle (feature, release, hotfix), main shows only releases. Your hashes will differ.

1.title: Three strategies and the team each one fits, continued
1.text: Three strategies and the team each one fits. Small team, strong automated tests, deploys many times a day. Trunk-based. Web app deployed from main, every change reviewed in a P R. Git Hub flow. Scheduled releases and several supported versions. Git Flow or release branches. Tip: Start with Git Hub flow and add complexity only when a real need appears. Every extra long-lived branch is more merging.

1.title: Release branches and hotfixes
1.text: Release branches and hotfixes. A release branch such as release slash one dot two is cut from the release tag and stays alive while that version is supported. A hotfix repairs a bug found in a shipped version. It takes three moves. Branch hotfix slash rounding from release slash one dot two, and commit the fix. Merge it into release slash one dot two with the no ff flag, and tag v one dot two dot one. Copy the fix to main with git cherry pick dash x, which records the source commit in the message. One bug means one fix on every line that has it. In Git Flow the hotfix goes into main and develop.

1.title: Release branches and hotfixes, continued
1.text: Release branches and hotfixes. Try it. Fix a shipped version and carry the fix to main. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Release branches and hotfixes, continued
1.text: Release branches and hotfixes. The copy on main is a new commit with a new hash. Two results can surprise you. git describe on main still counts from v one.two point zero, because v one.two point one is not reachable from main. And git branch dash d hotfix slash rounding refuses on main, because the hotfix commit itself is not in main. Delete it while on release slash one dot two. Tip: Use git cherry pick dash x when you copy a fix. The "cherry picked from" line lets anyone trace the copy back to the original.

1.title: Branch names and long-lived branches
1.text: Branch names and long-lived branches. Keep names short, lowercase and descriptive, with a prefix for the purpose. feature slash. Use: New work. Sample: feature slash one hundred twenty-three cart totals. fix slash. Use: Ordinary bug fix. Sample: fix slash login redirect. hotfix slash. Use: Urgent production fix. Sample: hotfix slash rounding. release slash. Use: Release preparation or support. Sample: release slash one dot two.

1.title: Branch names and long-lived branches, continued
1.text: Branch names and long-lived branches. Git refuses spaces and.. in a name. It also refuses a branch named feature while feature slash cart exists, because branches are stored as paths: the error is cannot lock ref. A long-lived branch drifts away from main. Every day it costs more: conflicts grow, reviews get bigger, and nobody else sees the work. Measure the drift and test the merge early. Try it. Count how far apart two branches are, then try the merge.

1.title: Branch names and long-lived branches, continued
1.text: Branch names and long-lived branches. The numbers are commits only in main (four) and only in the branch (one). The cure: merge main in often, cut the work into small P Rs, and hide unfinished work behind flags. Release branches are long-lived on purpose, but take fixes only.

1.title: Tags, versions and releases
1.text: Tags, versions and releases. A tag is a permanent name for one commit. An annotated tag stores the tagger, the date and a message, so use it for releases. A lightweight tag is only a name; git cat file dash t prints tag for the first kind and commit for the second. A plain git push sends branches, not tags. Send one tag with git push origin v one dot two dot zero, or all with the tags flag. A fresh clone then has them.

2.title: Tags, versions and releases, continued
2.text: Tags, versions and releases. git describe the tags flag names a commit from the nearest tag. On the tag it prints the tag. Two commits later it prints v one dot two dot zero to two g seven one seven b eight seven one: the tag, the commits since it, and g plus the short hash. Try it. Tag a release, describe it before and after two more commits, and push it.

2.title: Tags, versions and releases, continued
2.text: Tags, versions and releases. Semantic versioning writes versions as major.minor.patch, and a lower number resets when a higher one rises. major. Rises when: A breaking change forces users to adapt. Sample: one point two.three becomes two point zero.zero. minor. Rises when: A new feature that stays backward compatible. Sample: one point two.three becomes one point three.zero. patch. Rises when: A backward compatible bug fix. Sample: one point two.three becomes one point two.four.

2.title: Tags, versions and releases, continued
2.text: Tags, versions and releases. A plain git tag sorts by name, so v one dot ten dot zero appears before v one dot two dot zero. Sort by version instead. Try it. List three tags by name, then by version. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

2.title: Tags, versions and releases, continued
2.text: Tags, versions and releases. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

2.title: Tags, versions and releases, continued
2.text: Tags, versions and releases. A Git Hub release is based on a Git tag. Managing releases needs write permission. The notes can be written by hand or generated from a template, and Git Hub attaches the source as a zip file and a tarball. A release can hold up to one thousand assets, each under two gibibytes B. Tip: Tag every release with an annotated tag, and push it by name. Releases, git describe and rollbacks all depend on tags that really exist.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Ada's team deploys main many times a day. A new checkout is unfinished, but its first pieces should merge now. What lets them do it safely? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Merge the code behind a feature flag that is switched off. A feature flag lets unfinished code live in main without users seeing it.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A bug is reported in the shipped v one.two point zero, and main already holds one point three work. Where does the fix belong? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: On a branch from release slash one dot two, tag v one.two point one, then copy to main. Fix the supported line first, tag it, and copy the fix to every other line that has the bug.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. git describe the tags flag prints v one dot four dot zero to three g nine a one b two c three. What does that tell you? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: head is three commits after the tag v one.four point zero, at commit nine a one b two c three. The format is the tag, the commits since it, and g plus the short hash.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. The shop is at two point three.four. A release removes a function that other teams call. Which version comes next? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: three point zero.zero, because a breaking change raises major. A breaking change raises major and resets minor and patch to zero.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Bob tagged version two.zero point zero and ran git push. Teammates cannot see the tag on Git Hub. What is the fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Run git push origin version two dot zero dot zero, as a plain push sends no tags. A plain git push sends branches only, so the tag must be pushed by name.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A team ships packaged software on a schedule and supports versions one.x and two point x at the same time. Which approach fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Release branches per version, tagged, with hotfixes to each. Several supported versions need a branch and tags for each, and a hotfix for each affected line.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Name the five branch types of Git Flow. Answer: main, develop, feature, release and hotfix. Question two. When does the minor number rise? Answer: When a backward compatible feature is added; patch resets to zero. Question three. Which command creates an annotated tag? Answer: git tag dash a v one dot two dot zero dash m message.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which command sends one tag to the remote? Answer: git push origin v one dot two dot zero. Question five. What is a Git Hub release based on? Answer: A Git tag. Question six. Which command shows how far a branch has drifted from main? Answer: git rev list the left right flag the count flag, run on main dot dot dot branch.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Trunk-based: tiny branches, merge often, feature flags hide unfinished work. Git Hub flow: one short branch per change, P R, merge, deploy from main. Git Flow: main, develop, feature, release, hotfix; releases tagged on main. Hotfix: branch from the release, merge and tag, then git cherry pick dash x to main. Branch names: prefix and short description; no spaces; feature clashes with feature slash cart. Long-lived branches: drift and conflicts; measure with git rev list the left right flag the count flag. Tags: git tag dash a, then git push origin tag; a plain push sends none. Semantic versions: major breaking, minor feature, patch fix. describe: tag N ghash means N commits after the tag. Git Hub release: based on a tag; notes by hand or template; source zip and tarball added.
